newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Annan says Cyprus accord "within our grasp".
newsitem.headline: Annan says Cyprus accord "within our grasp".

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Wednesday that an end to the division of Cyprus was within reach but the consequences of failure could be more dire than at any time in recent decades.

Annan was opening five days of U.N.-sponsored talks between the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, President Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Denktash, aimed at reviving negotiations on establishing a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
"I invited the leaders of the Cypriot communities to meet here for face-to-face talks because I believe that a lasting peace in Cyprus is now within our grasp," Annan said at an opening ceremony.
The talks are being held at a picturesque resort called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 km) north of New York.
Annan said his special envoy for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, would be submitting "a number of suggestions" to facilitate their work.

"If you agree with these suggestions, you will be sending a strong and unmistakable signal to the international community. You will be signalling your commitment and determination to reach a comprehensive settlement -- for which the people of Cyprus have been waiting for too long," he said.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since troops from Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

But the Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence that resulted in the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force that is still on the island.
In his speech, Annan said young Cypriots were growing up under a "cloud of uncertainty and potential instability".
"For their sake, this cannot continue. There is a sense of greater urgency, more of a consensus than ever that this dispute must be brought to an end," he said.
"The consequences of failure are likely to be more dire than at any time in recent decades," he added, apparently alluding to forthcoming events that could precipitate a crisis.
These include talks expected to begin next year on European Union membership for Cyprus and the Nicosia government's planned deployment of Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles.

Turkey and the Turkish Cypriots, who do not recognise the Greek Cypriot-led Nicosia government, say it cannot negotiate EU membership for the entire island. Any move in that direction would result in linking northern Cyprus even more closely with Turkey, they say.
Turkey, with air bases little more than 40 miles (65 km) from Cyprus, has also said it would take any steps necessary to prevent the deployment next year of the S-300 missiles.
Annan said that the Cypriot communities would earn international respect and gratitude if they reached agreement.

The world would also be profoundly relieved "at the removal of a potential flashpoint from international relations in the Eastern Mediterranean." Most importantly, an accord would "provide a prosperous and peaceful future for all Cypriots."
Annan noted that the first Cyprus inter-communal talks were held 29 years ago -- led by Clerides and Denktash as presidents of their respective communal parliaments.
Efforts involving four previous U.N. secretaries-general had provided an approach for tackling crucial issues, he said.
"I strongly believe that what is needed now is to explore, without further delay, specific and concrete solutions to each of those issues, and to do so in their in their proper context.

"This can be achieved only if you begin consideration of the actual documents and legal instruments that will constitute the comprehensive settlement," he said, appealing to both sides to observe a news blackout until the talks end.
